title: Loadharness orchestration lab notes 2025
body:
Purpose and scope:

This note captures exploratory lab experiments and pragmatic heuristics for orchestrating loadgen runs across heterogeneous GPU pools. The emphasis is on improving repeatability of throughput claims while surface-profiling transient bottlenecks that standard warmup checklists miss. This is a working log — rough observations, config snippets, and next steps.

High-level problem statement:
- We often observe discrepant throughput between short validation runs and long-run plateaus.
- Causes appear multi-modal: hardware thermals/frequency scaling, kernel scheduler fragmentation, NVLINK/PCIe contention on multi-GPU nodes, and client-side pacing jitter.
- Existing warmup heuristics (seeded priming with fixed prefix) reduce variance but don't surface slow drift effects that appear after 30–90 minutes.

Core hypotheses tested in this lab:
1) GPU thermometry matters: transient downclocking and power capping after sustained bursts reduce plateau throughput even after traditional warmup.
2) Occupancy snapshots taken at critical phases (cold, post-priming, mid-plateau) reveal memory fragmentation and queue length changes that correlate with throughput drops.
3) Coordinating client RNG seeds and session affinity reduces outlier tail latency incidence and improves steady throughput by reducing cache miss churn.

Key instrumentation added for experiments:
- Continuous NVML thermometry stream (gpu_temp, gpu_power, sm_clock, mem_clock) at 1s resolution.
- Host-level perf counters: context-switch rates, irq rates, and PCIe throughput saturations (where available).
- Kernel-level timeline capture: per-inference kernel start/end timestamps and CUDA stream queue depths (via lightweight tracing).
- Loadgen-side: per-request metadata: seed, client_id, session_id, primed_bytes, token_count, KV_cache_hit (true/false).

Observed phenomena (summary):
- On a 4xA100 node, after repeated 2-minute microburst windows (100 qps effective), GPUs dip 50–120MHz on SM clocks after ~18 minutes. Plateaus measured after 60 minutes were ~6–9% lower than 5-minute runs.
- NVLINK counters showed periodic spikes coincident with initial model broadcasting (warmup fanout). When fanout overlapped with peak host PCIe usage (other workloads), observed higher variance in per-token latency.
- Session affinity (stick client sessions to the same worker) reduced KV cache miss rate by ~12% in our chat-eval workload and knocked down tail latency p99-p999 spread.

Novel procedures and config guidance (lab-grounded):
1) Thermometry-aware warmup:
   - Step 0: cold snapshot. Record baseline temps/clocks for each GPU for 30s idle.
   - Step 1: gradual priming: run 10x short priming sequences spaced 5s apart rather than one long priming blast. This staggers power ramp and reduces forced thermal throttles on some cards.
   - Step 2: hold at target throughput for an observation window (recommended: 12 minutes) and confirm stable SM clocks for the last 3 minutes of the window. If clock drift > 20MHz observed, extend window or add cool-down cycles.
   - Rationale: avoids transient downclocking being mistaken for benchmark noise.

2) Occupancy snapshot orchestration:
   - Capture three occupancy snapshots per run: cold, post-warmup, mid-plateau. Each snapshot is a short capture (5s) of kernel queue depths, GPU memory free/used, and CUDA stream counts.
   - Save snapshots with run-id and seed to enable comparison between runs. Store as CSV with columns: run_id,timestamp,gpu_id,sm_clock,mem_free,queued_kernels,stream_count.
   - Use diffs between post-warmup and mid-plateau to surface fragmentation (e.g., mem_free drops non-linearly relative to expected token footprint).

3) Seeded but randomized client pacing (seed hygiene):
   - Keep RNG seeds consistent across runs but vary deterministic offsets between client shards. This ensures repeatability but preserves inter-client phase variance to mimic production concurrency.
   - Avoid fully synchronized periodic bursts (all clients aligned on the same timing) — that pattern exposes hardware resonance and increases variance.

4) Salvage throughput check (post-tail recovery):
   - After a detected tail surge (p99>threshold), run a short salvage sequence: 30s at 25% of target throughput, then ramp back to target.
   - Measure time-to-recover (seconds until p50 and p95 return within 5% of pre-surge levels). Use this metric alongside raw throughput as a resilience covariate.

Recommended loadgen config template (example snippet used in lab):

# loadharness config (yaml-like for readability)
# note: fields shown as example strings in this doc. Actual CLI accepts JSON/YAML.
name: "chat-occupancy-e2e"
model: "redwood-open-v2-13b"
clients: 48
client_shards: 12
target_qps_per_client: 1.2
sequence_length: 512
session_affinity: true
seed_strategy: "deterministic-offsets"
priming: 
  prefix_sequences: 8
  spacing_seconds: 5
  reuse_kv: true
thermometry_probe_interval_seconds: 1
occupancy_snapshots: ["cold","post_warmup","mid_plateau"]
salvage_policy:
  enabled: true
  cooldown_qps_fraction: 0.25
  cooldown_duration_seconds: 30
  recovery_ramp_seconds: 60
metrics_export: "prometheus_pushgateway://benching/job/loadharness"

Practical thresholds learned from runs:
- Declare a run stable when: 1) 12-minute observation window with last 3 minutes SM clock variance < 20MHz and p50 throughput CV < 3% across 30s buckets.
- If salvage recovery time > 120s consistently, suspect host/resource interference (noisy neighbor) or kernel fragmentation; mark node as suspect for longer defrag/probing.

Experiment notes and reproducible sequence:
- Run A (2024-11-20): default priming (one-shot) at 80% target qps on a 8xA100 cluster. Result: 8% higher throughput on 5m run vs 60m run. Post-mortem: thermal drop at 22min.
- Run B (2024-12-02): applied gradual priming + thermometry checks + salvage policy. Result: 1.7% delta between 10m and 60m runs; salvage time median 18s.
- Run C (2025-01-04): toggled session_affinity=false to test cache effect. Observed KV cache miss increase and 14% p99 inflation.

Anomaly hunting checklist (quick):
- Check NVML logs for SM clock dips around the time throughput falls.
- Cross-reference host cpu-steal/irq with period of tail spikes.
- Inspect PCIe counters for saturations during warmup fanout.
- Confirm client seeds and request timestamps to rule out accidental synchronized bursts.

Next experiments (backlog):
- Test targeted cooler cycles: after 30m sustained runs, insert a 45s cooldown (50% qps) and measure whether throughput recovers better than passive salvage.
- Evaluate kernel fusion scheduling changes in runtime to reduce queued kernel spikes that signpost fragmentation.
- Explore micro-scheduling on client side: slight randomized jitter per-request (Gaussian sigma 6–12ms) to see if it reduces resonance effects without impacting p50.

Notes to reviewers:
- Configs and trace collection scripts are in the linked PR and the bench runner repo (see linked_artifacts).
- This doc intentionally mixes high-level heuristics and raw lab observations — we'll extract a condensed playbook for the benchmark runbook if reviewers agree on the thresholds above.

Quick reference TL;DR (for engineers running repeatable throughput claims):
- Use gradual priming spaced short bursts instead of single long priming blasts.
- Instrument thermometry and require SM clock stability in the last 3 minutes of your warmup observation window.
- Capture occupancy snapshots and store them with run metadata for post-run diffing.
- Keep seed hygiene: deterministic but offset between shards.
- Implement a salvage policy to gauge resilience and use recovery time as an additional metric when reporting throughput numbers.

-- Asha
